questions.stem:
A client attending a design meeting trips on a loose carpet seam in an architecture firm's conference room and fractures a wrist. The client files a claim against the firm.

Which of the firm's policies would respond first?

options.text: Professional liability
options.explanation: Professional liability covers negligent professional services, not premises injuries.

options.text: Commercial general liability
options.explanation: Correct. CGL covers bodily injury and property damage arising from the firm's premises and non-professional operations.

options.text: Workers' compensation
options.explanation: Workers' compensation covers the firm's own employees, not clients or visitors.

options.text: Umbrella liability
options.explanation: An umbrella adds limits above the CGL. It doesn't respond until the underlying CGL limit is used up.

questions.explanation: Match the loss to the policy: premises injury to a third party → CGL.

questions.stem:
An architect retires, closes her firm, and lets her claims-made professional liability policy expire. Two years later, a former client makes a claim about a project designed while the policy was in force.

Which coverage would have protected her against this claim?

options.text: An extended reporting period endorsement
options.explanation: Correct. A tail extends the time for reporting claims arising from work performed before the policy ended.

options.text: Prior acts coverage from a new carrier
options.explanation: Prior acts coverage preserves the retroactive date when switching carriers. It doesn't extend reporting after coverage ends.

options.text: An umbrella policy over the firm's coverage
options.explanation: Umbrella policies typically sit above CGL, auto and employer's liability, not professional liability.

options.text: Occurrence-based general liability
options.explanation: General liability excludes professional services regardless of trigger.

questions.explanation: Claims-made coverage responds to claims made during the policy period. A tail extends it after the policy ends.

questions.stem:
A firm engages a renderer under a written agreement that calls her an independent contractor.

Which facts indicate she may legally be an employee?

options.text: The firm sets her daily hours and requires her to work in its office.
options.explanation: Correct. Control over when and where the work is done points to employment.

options.text: The firm supplies her computer and software and trains her in its methods.
options.explanation: Correct. Providing tools and training shows behavioral and financial control.

options.text: She works only for this firm, full time, with no end date.
options.explanation: Correct. An ongoing, exclusive, full-time relationship reflects economic dependence.

options.text: She invoices per project at rates she sets.
options.explanation: Setting her own rates and invoicing by project points toward independent-contractor status.

options.text: The written agreement designates her an independent contractor.
options.explanation: The label isn't controlling. The actual working relationship decides.

options.text: She maintains her own business license and insurance.
options.explanation: Running her own business with its own license and insurance points toward independence.

questions.explanation: Classification turns on control and economic reality, not the contract's label.

questions.stem:
A non-exempt drafter works 46 hours in one workweek at a regular rate of $30 per hour.

Under federal law, what is the minimum gross pay for the week?

options.explanation: This leaves out the 6 hours worked beyond 40.
This pays all 46 hours at the regular rate, with no overtime premium.
This pays the 6 overtime hours at double time, which federal law doesn't require.

questions.explanation: FLSA: non-exempt employees earn at least 1.5 × their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek (29 U.S.C. §207).

questions.stem:
An employee strains his back while carrying sample boards to a client presentation.

Which statement about the firm's obligation is generally correct?

options.text: Workers' compensation provides benefits regardless of fault.
options.explanation: Correct. Workers' compensation is no-fault, and it's generally the employee's exclusive remedy against the employer.

options.text: The employee may also sue the firm for negligence.
options.explanation: Workers' compensation generally bars a separate negligence suit against the employer.

options.text: The firm's general liability policy covers his medical costs.
options.explanation: CGL policies typically exclude injuries to the insured's own employees.

options.text: Coverage applies only to injuries at the firm's office.
options.explanation: Work-related injuries away from the office, such as at a client meeting, are generally covered.

questions.explanation: Employee work injury → workers' compensation: no-fault, generally the exclusive remedy.

questions.stem:
A principal is reviewing the firm's professional liability policy before renewal.

Which statements about this type of coverage are generally true?

options.text: It is typically written on a claims-made basis.
options.explanation: Correct. Most architects' professional liability policies are claims-made.

options.text: Defense costs may reduce the available limit of liability.
options.explanation: Correct. Many policies have eroding limits, where defense spending reduces the remaining limit.

options.text: It covers bodily injury to visitors at the firm's office.
options.explanation: Premises injuries fall under commercial general liability.

options.text: It covers guarantees of performance written into contracts.
options.explanation: Liability assumed by contract beyond the negligence standard is generally excluded.

options.text: It responds to claims made after the policy expires.
options.explanation: Claims-made coverage requires the claim during the policy period, or within an extended reporting period.

options.text: It pays to correct the contractor's defective workmanship.
options.explanation: Contractor workmanship is the contractor's responsibility under its contract and warranty.

questions.explanation: Professional liability: negligence in professional services, claims-made, limits may erode, contractual guarantees excluded.

questions.stem:
A 30-person firm's project manager, employed full time for three years, asks for eight weeks off to care for a parent with a serious health condition. The firm has no other offices.

What does federal law require of the firm?

options.text: None, because of the firm's size
options.explanation: Correct. The FMLA applies to employers with 50 or more employees (29 U.S.C. §2611(4)). State law or firm policy may still provide leave.

options.text: Up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave
options.explanation: That describes FMLA leave, but the FMLA doesn't cover an employer this size.

options.text: Up to 12 weeks of paid family leave
options.explanation: The FMLA provides unpaid leave and doesn't cover this employer.

options.text: Leave only after 12 months of continuous service
options.explanation: Service length is one eligibility test, but the employer-size threshold isn't met.

questions.explanation: Know the federal thresholds: FMLA 50+, COBRA and ADEA 20+, Title VII and ADA 15+.

questions.stem:
An architect sends a junior designer to document existing conditions at an occupied building where the contractor has begun selective demolition.

Which action is most appropriate for the firm?

options.text: Provide PPE and training, and require site-rule compliance.
options.explanation: Correct. The firm protects its own employee as an employer, while the contractor remains responsible for site safety overall.

options.text: Rely on the contractor's site safety program to protect the designer.
options.explanation: The contractor controls the site, but the firm still has OSHA employer duties to its own staff.

options.text: Direct the contractor to suspend demolition during the visit.
options.explanation: Directing the contractor's operations moves means-and-methods and safety responsibility onto the architect.

options.text: Have the designer sign a waiver before entering the site.
options.explanation: A waiver doesn't satisfy the firm's safety duties or affect workers' compensation rights.

questions.explanation: Protect your own staff without taking control of the contractor's site safety (A201-2017 §3.3.1, Art. 10).

questions.stem:
A firm is moving its claims-made professional liability coverage to a new insurance carrier.

Which provision should the firm make sure the new policy includes?

options.text: The original retroactive date
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping the original retroactive date means claims about earlier work stay covered (prior acts coverage).

options.text: A retroactive date matching the new policy's start
options.explanation: That would leave all earlier work uninsured for future claims.

options.text: An occurrence-based coverage form
options.explanation: Occurrence-based professional liability is rarely available. Continuity of claims-made coverage is the practical protection.

options.text: A lower per-claim deductible
options.explanation: The deductible affects cost sharing, not the coverage gap for prior work.

questions.explanation: When changing carriers, preserve the retroactive date.

questions.stem:
An employee drives her own car to a site visit and causes an accident that injures the other driver.

Which coverages are most likely to respond to the other driver's claim?

options.text: The employee's personal auto policy
options.explanation: Correct. The vehicle owner's auto policy is typically primary.

options.text: The firm's hired and non-owned auto coverage
options.explanation: Correct. It protects the firm when employees use personal vehicles on firm business.

options.text: The firm's professional liability policy
options.explanation: Driving isn't a professional service.

options.text: The firm's workers' compensation policy
options.explanation: Workers' compensation covers the firm's employees, not third parties.

options.text: The firm's commercial general liability policy
options.explanation: CGL policies typically exclude auto liability.

options.text: The project owner's builder's risk policy
options.explanation: Builder's risk covers physical loss to the work under construction.

questions.explanation: Employees' personal vehicles on firm business are a common gap, filled by hired and non-owned auto coverage.

flashcards.back: Claims alleging negligent acts, errors or omissions in professional services. Usually claims-made; may have eroding limits.
Bodily injury and property damage from non-professional operations or premises. Usually occurrence-based. Excludes professional services.
The policy in force when the claim is made responds, as long as the act happened after the retroactive date.
The policy in force when the injury or damage occurred responds, even if the claim comes years later.
Extended reporting period bought when a claims-made policy ends (retirement or closure) for later claims about past work.
Keeping the original retroactive date when switching carriers so earlier work stays insured.
State-mandated, no-fault coverage for employee work injuries; generally the employee's exclusive remedy against the employer.
Non-exempt employees: 1.5× regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek.

flashcards.front: What makes an employee exempt from overtime
flashcards.back: Both a duties test (e.g., learned professional) and salary basis at no less than $684/week (29 C.F.R. §541.600). Title alone doesn't count.

flashcards.front: Employee vs. independent contractor: deciding factor
flashcards.back: Control (behavioral, financial) and economic dependence, not the contract label.
Title VII & ADA: 15+. ADEA & COBRA: 20+. FMLA & ACA mandate: 50+. (States often cover smaller employers.)
Protects the firm when employees use personal or rented vehicles on firm business.
Employment practices liability: discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination claims.

flashcards.front: Who is responsible for jobsite safety?
flashcards.back: The contractor (A201-2017 §3.3.1, Art. 10). The architect protects its own staff but shouldn't take control of site safety.
Employers with 20+ employees; coverage generally 18 months after a qualifying event; the employee can be charged up to 102% of the premium.
